data.title: NovaTech Founders Permanently Banned From Crypto Industry After $1.37 Billion Judgment Over Ponzi Scheme Targeting Haitian Immigrants
data.description:
New York authorities have secured a $1.37 billion judgment against the founders of collapsed cryptocurrency platform NovaTech, following a fraud scheme that allegedly drained the savings of hundreds of thousands of investors worldwide.

We won a historic $1.3 billion judgment against the founders of crypto company NovaTech for defrauding hundreds of thousands of people, including Haitian immigrants in New York.

We'll always fight to bring fraudsters who take advantage of New Yorkers to justice.

— NY AG James (@NewYorkStateAG) November 25, 2026

The case centres on how the company used religious and immigrant communities to attract investors with promises of high returns, leaving thousands unable to recover their money.

NovaTech Founders Ordered To Pay $1.37 Billion

New York Attorney General Letitia James announced that a court had ordered NovaTech founders Cynthia and Eddy Petion to pay $1,367,023,585 for their roles in the scheme.

The judgment covers approximately $1.13 billion in disgorgement and $232.5 million in prejudgment interest.

🚨 NY AG @NewYorkStateAG Secures $1.37B Judgment Against NovaTech Founders Cynthia and Eddy Petion

​New York Attorney General Letitia James won a 1.37Bjudgment
1.135B disgorgement and $232.5M interest over the NovaTech and AWS Mining scheme after a prior default ruling and… pic.twitter.com/Ev0zL1F6e9

— Saint | Web3 | Data Analyst 📊 (@saintuc_eth) November 26, 2026

The scheme affected hundreds of thousands of investors worldwide, including approximately 11,000 New York residents.

Authorities said the company particularly targeted Haitian immigrant communities, using their religious and social networks to build trust and attract funds.

James said,

"NovaTech cruelly targeted immigrant families through faith and community groups with the promise of a better life while robbing them of their life savings."

The couple and related companies were also permanently barred from participating in the securities, commodities and cryptocurrency industries.

$1.37 billion. That's the price tag of NovaTech's alleged crypto Ponzi empire.

A US court has ordered NovaTech founders Cynthia Petion and Eddy Petion to pay approximately $1.37 billion in restitution and disgorgement of illicit profits, according to New York Attorney General… pic.twitter.com/tS0czBTVw6

— Brainrot Labs (@Brainrot_Labs) November 25, 2026

How NovaTech Used Religious Communities To Recruit Investors

New York authorities filed their lawsuit against NovaTech and cryptocurrency mining company AWS Mining in June 2024, accusing both businesses of operating illegal pyramid schemes.

According to the lawsuit, the companies recruited investors through church prayer groups, social media platforms and WhatsApp communities, particularly targeting Haitian immigrants.

They allegedly promised high returns from cryptocurrency and foreign exchange trading to encourage people to invest and bring in more participants.

The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) separately charged the Petions and NovaTech promoters with fraud in August 2024.

The regulator alleged that NovaTech collected more than $650 million in cryptocurrency assets from over 200,000 investors between 2019 and 2023.

Today we announced charges against Cynthia and Eddy Petion and their company, NovaTech Ltd., for operating a fraudulent scheme that raised more than $650 million in crypto assets from 200,000+ investors, including many in the Haitian-American community. https://t.co/MraCGrWeTO

— U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (@SECGov) August 12, 2024

However, most of the funds were allegedly used to pay earlier investors and recruitment commissions rather than being invested in financial markets as promised.

NovaTech eventually shut down in May 2023 after investors encountered difficulties withdrawing their money.

The SEC said most participants were unable to recover their investments.

Petions Fled The Country Before The Court Ruling

The $1.37 billion judgment follows a default ruling issued against the couple in August 2025 after they failed to respond to the lawsuit.

The Petions had reportedly left the US, with reports indicating that they were living in Panama when James filed the case in June 2024.

NovaTech founders Cynthia and Eddy Petion

Following the default ruling, the court proceeded to determine the amount the couple owed.

James' office requested approximately $1.37 billion in damages in October 2026.

Court documents also showed that the Petions failed to comply with an order requiring them to provide a full accounting of payments made to and received from investors.

Despite the judgment, recovering the money could prove difficult given that the couple had reportedly fled the country.

Four NovaTech Promoters Also Ordered To Pay Nearly $6 Million

The case also resulted in financial penalties against four other individuals involved in the scheme.

Martin Zizi, Frantz Ciceron, Ricardo Roy Sr. and James Corbett were ordered to pay nearly $6 million combined and permanently banned from participating in the securities, commodities and cryptocurrency industries.

Separately, Cynthia Petion and AWS Mining were ordered to pay a further $6.2 million combined over the AWS Mining scheme, according to the court proceedings.

James said the judgment would provide some justice to the victims who lost their savings through the operation, although her office has not specified how much of the $1.37 billion it expects to recover from the Petions.

data.title: Quick overview of the State Council executive meeting on November 27
data.description:
November 27, 2026State Council Executive Meeting Content.

I. Hearing a report on the comprehensive inspection of promoting high-quality development

The meeting pointed out that it is necessary to thoroughly address the problems discovered during the inspection, draw inferences from one instance to others, and promote the resolution of problems in a comprehensive manner to ensure the high-quality completion of all annual targets and tasks.

  • It is necessary to actively absorb the opinions and suggestions put forward by various localities, take them into consideration when studying the work plan for next year, and effectively improve related work.

    • Taking the inspection and rectification as an opportunity, we should strengthen the construction of long-term mechanisms, adjust and improve policies and measures that are not adapted to the requirements of high-quality development, optimize implementation methods, improve incentive and restraint mechanisms, and implement a comprehensive policy package. II. Studying the Continuous Deepening of Comprehensive Reform of Investment and Financing in the Capital Market The meeting pointed out that the capital market is crucial to the overall economic development. We must adhere to a goal-oriented and problem-oriented approach, simultaneously address counter-cyclical adjustments and reform efforts, continuously improve the capital market stabilization mechanism, effectively implement existing policies, plan and introduce new policies, and promote the stable and healthy development of the capital market. We must encourage listed companies to increase their dividend payouts and share buybacks, strengthen the role of the "national team" in stabilizing the market, further optimize the "stabilization fund" function of Central Huijin Investment Ltd., and provide ample liquidity guarantees. We must improve policies to support and guide the entry of medium- and long-term funds such as insurance, corporate annuities, and social security funds into the market, and continuously strengthen the power of medium- and long-term investment. We must strengthen the prevention and response to imported risks. We must enhance the endogenous driving force for high-quality development of the capital market through deepening reforms and accelerate the development of a multi-tiered capital market. We must strengthen the supervision of the entire capital market chain in accordance with the law, resolutely investigate and punish financial fraud, illegal share reduction and other behaviors, and effectively protect the legitimate rights and interests of investors. III. Hearing a report on the construction of the national standards system. The meeting pointed out that we must systematically optimize the standards system, promote the orderly transformation of industry standards into national standards, clean up and abolish local standards that do not meet the requirements of building a unified national market, and strengthen the guidance and regulation of group standards. We must strengthen the supply of high-quality standards, proactively plan the layout of standards for emerging and future industries, accelerate the updating of existing standards, shorten the standard formulation and revision cycle, and fill the gaps in mandatory standards in a targeted manner. IV. The meeting reviewed and approved the "Regulations on the Investigation and Management of Production Safety Accident Hazards (Draft)". The meeting pointed out that it is necessary to further strengthen and standardize the investigation and management of production safety hazards, and promote the transformation of the management model towards pre-accident prevention. It is necessary to focus on key industries and fields, implement closed-loop management of accident hazard rectification and delisting, and resolutely curb the occurrence of major and serious accidents. It is necessary to improve the professionalism and standardization of investigation and management, refine the criteria for judging major accident hazards, and promote the application of new digital technologies and equipment. The meeting emphasized the need to tighten and implement responsibilities at all levels, strengthen departmental supervision and management, and effectively safeguard the lives and property of the people. The meeting also discussed other matters.

data.title: Storage stocks strangle South Korean retail investors
data.description:
Author: Su Yang, Tencent Technology

The global memory chip market is experiencing an unprecedented price surge.

AI data centers are making massive purchases of memory chips, with Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology's production capacity being pre-booked. The price of some memory chips has increased tenfold in the past year. Electronics manufacturers are scrambling to find suppliers to secure supplies, and some products have even had to raise prices and reduce specifications.

While the supply chain is busy scrambling for supplies, the capital market is selling off memory stocks.

On November 25th local time, SK Hynix's stock price fell 11.05%, Samsung Electronics fell 9.87%, and the Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) fell more than 6%. Storage stocks, which had previously benefited from the continued surge in AI demand, suddenly experienced a concentrated sell-off. On one hand, there is a shortage of chips, with manufacturers' orders booked for years to come; on the other hand, investors are worried that high profits are unsustainable. Institutions such as Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley have already turned their attention to 2028, assessing the potential changes in storage prices and corporate profits after the release of new production capacity. AI demand continues to drive up storage chip prices, but the stock market has already cooled down this boom cycle in advance. How long will the storage chip shortage last? The most direct driver of this storage shortage comes from AI data centers. Large technology companies are continuously building AI infrastructure, requiring the purchase of large quantities of DRAM and high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Compared to traditional consumer electronics customers, cloud computing giants have more funds and make larger purchases. To secure supply, they are willing to sign long-term contracts and even lock in capacity for the next few years in advance. SK Hynix is ​​one of the main beneficiaries of this demand growth. The company holds a significant market share in the HBM field, and the demand for high-bandwidth memory from AI chip manufacturers such as Nvidia has brought it a large number of orders. As AI servers continue to expand, storage manufacturers are facing increasingly tight capacity. SK Hynix's memory chips are installed on memory modules. The pressure from AI demand has also spread to the traditional memory market. Because HBM is more profitable, manufacturers are investing more production resources in this area. However, HBM manufacturing involves complex processes and packaging, and its production resources, equipment, and capital investment compete with traditional DRAM, thus squeezing out the general memory needed by consumer electronics manufacturers. Expanding production capacity also cannot quickly alleviate the shortage. While Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology are all increasing investment, building new wafer fabs requires significant time for construction, equipment installation, process debugging, and capacity ramp-up. It takes considerable time from initial investment to effective supply. A November 25th report in the Wall Street Journal stated that some electronics manufacturers have established dedicated teams to procure memory chips, even resorting to secondhand trading platforms like eBay to find inventory. Some companies have had to readjust their procurement plans to secure supplies from Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The rising memory prices are also beginning to impact the consumer market. Apple has raised prices on some MacBooks, and the starting price of the iPhone 18 Pro series has increased; Microsoft's Xbox, Amazon's Echo Dot, and Meta Quest are also facing cost pressures. Some manufacturers have opted to reduce device memory configurations; Motorola has reduced the storage capacity of some models from 256GB to 128GB, without a corresponding price reduction. Some popular electronic products have seen price increases due to rising memory costs. However, demand is not growing in all sectors. A storage industry report released by GF Securities on November 26, citing TrendForce data, stated that Chinese cloud service providers have recently slowed their procurement pace, with insufficient GPU supply being one reason. Adjustments to related server DRAM orders account for approximately 1% of global DRAM demand, and procurement by US cloud service providers is expected to absorb this shortfall. The situation in the consumer market is even more noteworthy. Some customers have cut orders for enterprise-grade solid-state drives (eSSDs), and consumer electronics manufacturers have begun to reduce memory configurations, thus weakening demand for consumer-grade DRAM, with DDR4 being particularly affected. Guangfa Securities has consequently lowered its 2027 DRAM contract price forecast. Previously, the institution predicted that prices would rise by 10%, 7%, 5%, and 3% quarter-on-quarter in the four quarters of next year; the latest forecast has been lowered to 6%, 3%, 0%, and 0%. According to this forecast, DRAM prices will continue to rise in the first half of next year, and remain basically flat in the second half. However, the slowdown in price increases does not necessarily mean that supply is sufficient. Guangfa Securities still expects a supply gap of 5%, 5%, and 4% in the DRAM market from 2026 to 2028. HBM continues to occupy wafer capacity, and major manufacturers remain cautious about expanding traditional DRAM production, resulting in an overall tight supply. The shortage is also reflected in manufacturers' order cycles. SK Hynix has already sold its DRAM capacity up to 2029, and Micron has also secured a large supply in advance through multi-year contracts. SK Hynix CFO Kim Woo-hyun previously stated that the supply constraints may continue until 2030. However, there are differing opinions among institutions regarding how long the supply shortage will last. Nomura Securities believes that AI infrastructure construction will continue to support storage demand, and the supply shortage may continue until 2028. Goldman Sachs predicts that the DRAM supply-demand gap will narrow from 5.1% in 2027 to 1.2% in 2028, with traditional DRAM and NAND prices potentially falling by about 20% respectively. Stock Prices Diverge from Demand While memory chip prices are still rising, SK Hynix's stock price has already fallen sharply. Behind these two trends lies the different judgments of the industry's current demand and the capital market's assessment of future profitability. The memory industry has a clear cyclical nature. When supply is tight, manufacturers can raise prices, and profits increase accordingly; as new capacity is gradually released, the supply-demand relationship may reverse, and chip prices and profit margins will fall accordingly. This is precisely what investors are worried about. While SK Hynix benefits from HBM demand, its traditional DRAM and NAND businesses still impact its overall performance. Whether HBM business growth can fully offset this impact if traditional memory prices decline in the coming years remains uncertain. Guangfa Securities' calculations for 2028 demonstrate the potential downside for memory prices. Using a 2027 traditional DRAM price of $16 per GB as a benchmark, the firm calculated three scenarios: if prices return to pre-AI demand levels, they could fall to $4 per GB; based on long-term contract prices, approximately $8; and if demand remains strong, they could remain at $12. The corresponding declines are 75%, 50%, and 25%, respectively. HBM prices also have room to decline. Guangfa Securities predicts that the price per GB in 2028 may be between $20.7 and $29.6, 0% to 30% lower than the $29.6 in 2027. However, Guangfa Securities is not bearish on major storage manufacturers. The institution remains optimistic about Micron, SK Hynix, and Samsung Electronics, believing that if demand continues to weaken and prices begin to fall, major manufacturers may control supply by reducing production to prevent further price declines. Expectations for AI infrastructure investment have also seen significant adjustments recently. On November 26, research firm SemiAnalysis released a report that significantly lowered its forecasts for future AI computing power investment. The report projects that global AI accelerator capital expenditure will fall to $758 billion in 2028 from the previously forecast $1.04 trillion, a decrease of approximately 28%; chip spending in 2030 is projected to drop to $923 billion from $1.53 trillion, a decrease of 40%. The report also lowered its forecasts for chip shipments and energy demand. According to the latest forecasts, AI chip shipments between 2026 and 2030 will be 17% lower than previously expected, with HBM shipments expected to decline by 30%. South Korean brokerages have diverged in their market outlook. Daol Investment Securities believes that the recent stock price correction is too drastic relative to the company's fundamentals, maintaining a buy rating on SK Hynix with a fair value of 2 million won. BNK Investment & Securities lowered its target price to 1.05 million won, anticipating that customers and distributors will begin adjusting their inventories in the second and third quarters of next year, potentially leading to a significant drop in memory chip prices. Overseas investment banks are also lowering their forecasts. Goldman Sachs lowered its target price for SK Hynix from 3.5 million won to 2 million won, but maintained a buy rating. Morgan Stanley lowered its target price from 2.6 million won to 1.6 million won, warning of a potential "profit cliff" in 2028. Morgan Stanley also lowered its long-term average operating profit margin forecast for SK Hynix from 2029 to 2035 from 53% to 28%, reflecting its concerns about the long-term profitability of the memory industry. Not all institutions are bearish. Nomura Securities maintains its target price of 4.7 million won for SK Hynix, believing that the demand driven by AI infrastructure construction is sufficient to support supply shortages for an extended period. The core disagreement among institutions is not about whether AI still needs memory chips, but rather whether demand growth can continue to outpace supply expansion, and how long the high profits generated during the shortage period can be sustained. Stock prices have already begun to reflect these concerns, but the current shortage situation in the industry remains unchanged. Who is facing margin calls? The sharp fluctuations in memory stocks have also caused heavy losses for South Korean leveraged investors who bet on an upward trend. On November 25th, several SK Hynix single-stock leveraged ETFs in the South Korean market fell by more than 21%. The RISE SK Hynix single-stock leveraged ETF fell 22.78%, the KIWOOM SK Hynix Futures Single-Stock Leveraged ETF fell 22.21%, and similar products under SOL and KODEX fell 21.84% and 21.72% respectively. This is not the first time South Korean retail investors have suffered heavy losses in leveraged trading of storage stocks. According to data submitted to the National Assembly by the Financial Supervisory Service of Korea, from May 27th, when single-stock leveraged products were launched, to August 14th, individual investors suffered cumulative losses of 6.313 trillion won on single-stock leveraged and inverse products related to Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. Of this, realized losses amounted to 2.3242 trillion won, while unsold products showed a paper loss of 3.9888 trillion won. Investors of all ages were affected. Investors in their 40s suffered the largest cumulative losses, approximately 2.053 trillion won; those in their 50s suffered losses of approximately 1.8655 trillion won. Investors over 70 years old lost an average of approximately 29.94 million won per account. The drawdowns of individual products were even more dramatic. South Korean financial media outlet Edaily reported on November 6 that the SOL SK Hynix single-stock leveraged ETF closed at 3,340 won that day, a drop of approximately 91% from its high point on June 22. A similar product on KODEX fell from 44,000 won to around 4,000 won, also a drop of over 90%. The TIGER product experienced a similar decline. South Korean media had previously reported that some retail investors continued to buy leveraged products during the decline in storage stocks, hoping to lower their average cost and wait for a rebound. The concentrated sell-off on November 25 inflicted even greater losses on these investors.

Stablecoin Critic Hernández de Cos Set to Replace Lagarde as ECB President

Hernández de Cos, a former governor of Spain's central bank, has secured the backing of eurozone governments to succeed Christine Lagarde as ECB president after the Netherlands withdrew its support for rival candidate Klaas Knot, a former governor of the Dutch central bank.

🇪🇺 LATEST: Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos has been picked by eurozone countries to succeed Christine Lagarde as ECB president when she steps down on Feb. 7. https://t.co/BAMHU8K1ZS

— Cointelegraph (@Cointelegraph) November 27, 2026

The European Council put forward Hernández de Cos for the position on November 26, following the Council's recommendation. He is expected to take office on February 7, 2027, when Lagarde leaves the role, although the appointment still requires consultations with the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council before a formal decision.

Congratulations to Pablo Hernandez de Cos for earning the support of the EU Council to become ECB’s next President, and to Laurence Boone and Markus Brunnermeier for being recommended to join ECB’s Executive Board!

— Kristalina Georgieva (@KGeorgieva) November 26, 2026

His potential elevation comes with particular significance for the cryptocurrency industry, given his skepticism toward stablecoins and preference for alternative forms of digital money.

Hernández de Cos Questions Stablecoins' Viability for Mainstream Payments

Speaking at the Jackson Hole Economic Symposium in August, Hernández de Cos questioned whether stablecoins in their current form could become a credible means of payment at scale, arguing that tokenized bank deposits offer a more promising alternative for everyday transactions and wholesale settlement.

Pablo Hernández de Cos, un español al frente del Banco Central Europeo para dirigir la política monetaria de la eurozona. El relevo oficial se producirá tras la salida de Lagarde el 7 de febrero de 2027

— RTVE Noticias (@rtvenoticias) November 26, 2026

Although he acknowledged that stablecoins could serve specialized purposes, he warned that their widespread adoption could create broader risks for the traditional financial system.

In particular, he cautioned that growing reliance on US dollar-backed stablecoins outside the United States could undermine monetary sovereignty and weaken domestic monetary policy transmission. He also warned that a shift away from traditional bank deposits could increase banks' funding costs and potentially tighten lending conditions.

— Cointelegraph (@Cointelegraph) January 27, 2026

His position highlights the distinction between privately issued stablecoins and tokenized bank deposits, which represent commercial bank liabilities recorded on programmable digital platforms.

Rather than relying primarily on privately issued tokens, Hernández de Cos has argued for a monetary system that builds on tokenized deposits while preserving the role of central bank money in financial settlement.

Digital Euro Could Gain a Supporter as ECB Advances CBDC Plans

While Hernández de Cos has expressed reservations about stablecoins, he has been more receptive to central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), particularly the proposed digital euro.

In a 2023 speech, he argued that a digital euro could encourage innovation in payments while helping safeguard Europe's monetary sovereignty.

🇪🇺 BREAKING: The European Central Bank today published its Tokenisation Reference Model. The model serves as a framework for a single European tokenisation rulebook. https://t.co/wb1sB6m58A

His potential appointment comes as the ECB continues developing its digital euro initiative, with a pilot planned for 2027 and a potential launch in 2029, subject to legislative approval.

This creates an interesting contrast between his position on privately issued stablecoins and his support for a central bank-backed digital currency.

If confirmed, Hernández de Cos would take charge of the ECB as it advances its plans to introduce the digital euro, placing him at the center of Europe's efforts to modernize its payment infrastructure.

ECB Appointment Still Awaits Final Approval

Despite securing political backing, Hernández de Cos has yet to receive his formal appointment as ECB president. The European Council will first consult the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council before making its final decision, which is expected in December.

The selection followed negotiations between eurozone governments over Lagarde's successor. The Netherlands had initially backed Knot, but withdrew its support as Hernández de Cos secured the necessary backing from member states.

Lagarde announced in October that she would leave the ECB presidency on February 7, 2027, nine months before the scheduled end of her eight-year term.

Once formally appointed, Hernández de Cos will serve an eight-year, non-renewable term, leading the ECB through an important period for European monetary policy and the development of its digital currency infrastructure.

data.title: Musk is ramping up his spending spree: giving away another SpaceX share to every child in the US each year.
data.description:
Author: Bao Yilong, Wall Street Insights

Just yesterday, news broke that Musk would give every child in the US two shares of SpaceX stock, worth approximately $18 billion. Today, Musk has added to his investment on X.

On November 27th, Beijing time, Musk responded to a comment on the X platform, stating:

He will donate one more SpaceX stock to every American child every year.

This means that the already record-breaking "billion-dollar equity gift package" is transforming from a one-time donation into a long-term equity transfer year after year. Previously, Wall Street Insights reported that SpaceX announced it would donate one newly issued Class A common stock to every American child holding a "Trump account," and Musk subsequently pledged to donate an equal share in his personal capacity. The initial donation plan was valued at approximately $18 billion. With the addition of an annual donation mechanism, this largest-ever corporate and individual-directed equity distribution program is drawing widespread scrutiny from the capital market regarding equity dilution, lock-up period rules, and government-business interactions. Meanwhile, because the donated shares have a strict five-year mandatory lock-up period, millions of SpaceX shares will remain locked in children's accounts for an extended period, directly impacting the company's secondary market share structure after its IPO. Upgraded from "one-time matching donation" to annual continuous distribution. According to the initially announced plan, American children eligible for the "Trump Account" would receive two shares of SpaceX stock. One newly issued Class A common stock from SpaceX will be transferred next month; the other share, belonging to Musk personally, will be transferred after his personal lock-up period expires next June. Meanwhile, SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell and her husband had previously announced, through a related initiative of the Trump administration, that they would donate more than 2 million SpaceX shares to individuals in the account system. Data shows that since its launch in July of this year, the "Trump Account" has accumulated more than $9 billion in donations. Musk's additional commitment to "give away one more share every year" in the comments section of the X platform means that SpaceX shares held by American families will accumulate over time, and the total donation will continue to expand as the company's future valuation fluctuates. However, Musk has not yet disclosed further details regarding the specific implementation timeline for new annual donations, eligibility criteria, and the handling of minors after they reach adulthood. The timing of this large-scale equity donation highly coincides with policy adjustments by US regulators and SpaceX's business expansion. Shortly before announcing the increased donation, SpaceX had just received approval from US regulators to deploy up to 1 million satellites for building space data centers in low Earth orbit. Market analysis points out that as large technology companies face increasing public scrutiny due to the massive power consumption and environmental impact of their data centers, building computing infrastructure in space reflects Musk's strategic intention to extend his asset-heavy computing business beyond Earth, but also faces engineering challenges such as heat dissipation, energy supply, and orbital congestion. At the account system level, the US Treasury Department has also cleared legal obstacles in advance. Initially, the "Trump Account" was strictly limited to an index fund account, with legally mandated funds only allowed to invest in low-fee funds tracking U.S. stock market indices to prevent children's accounts from being exposed to individual stock volatility. However, on September 29th of this year, the U.S. Treasury Department issued new regulations establishing exemptions, explicitly stating that donated shares are not subject to regular investment restrictions, thus allowing the legal deposit of single-company stock into children's accounts. The lock-up period rule has sparked scrutiny from market participants. In discussions on social media platform X, while most ordinary netizens welcomed the free stock donations, some market observers questioned the underlying transaction structure and market impact. Renowned financial writer Ricardo analyzed on the X platform that this donation design objectively played a role in stabilizing SpaceX's stock price. According to new Treasury regulations, U.S. households cannot refuse to receive gifted stock, and the gifted stock must be held for at least 5 years, or until the end of the year the recipient child turns 17 (whichever is earlier); if the trustee sells the stock before the due date, the trustee must repurchase the same amount of stock. Ricardo further cited industry data and analysis, pointing out that June next year is the time when Musk's personal lock-up period expires, and he will transfer some of the shares that were originally freely tradable to children's accounts that will be subject to a five-year lock-up period. Ricardo believes this will help buffer potential pressure from insider selling: SpaceX needs this kind of help. SpaceX completed its IPO in June with an offering price of $135. Its stock price reached $201.80 on June 16th, but had fallen back to above $127 by Wednesday. Northern Trust expert Jane Ditelberg stated that such holding period restrictions objectively protect donors from the impact of concentrated selling leading to a drop in stock price. Furthermore, Ricardo cited an interpretation from the tax research firm Kitces, stating that donors can also be exempted from taxes related to unrealized capital gains on donated shares; while at the SpaceX company level, matching donations are made through the issuance of new shares, the cost of which is essentially borne by all existing shareholders through equity dilution.

Public Opinion Counterattack and Long-Term Return Calculation

In response to the above questions surrounding stock price protection and rule restrictions, a large number of rebuttals quickly appeared in the comment section of the X platform.

Some netizens bluntly stated that Ricardo's analyst's post was one of the dumbest posts on X.

Many commentators believe that if Musk's initial intention was merely to prevent the stock from flooding the secondary market and causing a market crash, he could have chosen to continue holding the shares personally, rather than transferring assets worth hundreds of billions of dollars to children across the United States free of charge. Many supporters argue that the mandatory five-year lock-up rule effectively helps families achieve long-term value investing, avoiding short-term speculative selling, and allowing the next generation to directly share in the growth dividends of leading aerospace and technology companies. Regarding earnings expectations, Musk previously commented on social media that if SpaceX successfully achieves its multi-planetary species goal and effectively utilizes solar energy, its long-term value will have enormous potential, therefore advising holders to continue holding their shares. Independent analyst ApoStructura also provided a quantitative calculation model on the X platform: If calculated at a rate of one new share added per year, even with an extremely conservative annual growth rate of 10%, the value of SpaceX stock in each American child's account would reach approximately $14,000 by the time they turn 18; If calculated at an annual growth rate of 20%, the average stock value per person would rise to approximately $68,000. The total market value held by children across the United States will exceed $1.1 trillion.

data.title: 1Password Hackers Steal Customer Data And Source Code, But Encrypted Vaults Remain Safe
data.description:
Hackers Exploited Employee GitHub Account to Breach 1Password Systems

The breach began after an attacker gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account, which provided a route into 1Password's internal development environment.

Yesterday @1Password confirmed a breach after hackers got in through one employee's GitHub account and pushed malicious code to copy customer records. Names, emails and sign in times are out there now, so expect some very convincing 1Password emails asking you to verify something. Remember, changing passwords is a good holiday chore.

— genuine (@GenuineDegen) November 26, 2026

The company said it began investigating the incident on Nov. 19 after discovering signs of unauthorized access to the employee's account. The attacker subsequently used the compromised account to access source code repositories and push malicious code into 1Password's backend services.

That code enabled the attacker to download administrative information associated with a subset of customers, including names, email addresses and other non-secret account metadata.

1/5 Everyone is talking about the 1Password incident today, and half the timeline is panicking while the other half is confused. Let's break down what actually happened and what to do next.

— Reinge (@CryptoReinge) November 26, 2026

According to 1Password, the stolen information also included account identifiers, account creation dates, last sign-in timestamps and public keys, which are designed to be publicly accessible.

The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and accessed the company's continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) environment, which is used to build and deploy software.

🚨 Bithumb thought hackers were inside its systems for 59 minutes. It turns out they had access for 15 days. The crypto exchange now confirms a wider breach involving sensitive personal and financial data. Here's what changed in its disclosure: https://t.co/PDu0cMg22i https://t.co/bwMN3Ofp0N

— The Hacker News (@TheHackersNews) November 26, 2026

This access potentially exposed internal infrastructure credentials, adding another layer of concern to the incident. 1Password subsequently rotated credentials that may have been exposed during the breach.

The password manager is used by millions of people and more than 200,000 businesses, making the incident particularly significant for customers who rely on the platform to protect their digital credentials.

1Password Says Customer Vaults and Encryption Keys Remain Secure

Despite the attacker gaining access to internal systems and customer account information, 1Password said its core password vault infrastructure was not compromised.

The company confirmed that customer vault contents, the cryptographic keys protecting them and account recovery keys were not accessed or exposed during the incident.

A key reason is that 1Password does not store customers' account passwords or Secret Keys on its backend systems. These security mechanisms help protect the encryption of customer vaults, preventing an attacker who gains access to backend infrastructure from simply opening users' stored passwords and other sensitive information.

There’s no need for scaremongering, but claiming all customer vaults are secure goes a little too far. High value targets could already have had their devices compromised, exposing their Account Passwords and Secret Keys. If attackers obtained their encrypted vault data through this breach, they could combine the two to decrypt entire vaults. That’s a technically possible worst case scenario, and well resourced threat actors have every incentive to target valuable individuals. Would really appreciate your feedback so I can update my posts across LinkedIn and Substack. Wishing you the very best during this tough time!

— Paul Walsh (@Paul__Walsh) November 26, 2026

As a result, 1Password said there was no evidence that customer accounts had been taken over or compromised and that users did not need to change their account credentials because of the incident.

The company also said its applications and browser extensions continued operating normally.

The incident nevertheless highlights the risks of attacks targeting the internal systems and developer accounts that support widely used security services. Even when encryption protects customer data, compromised employee credentials can still give attackers access to sensitive information and software infrastructure.

Stolen Customer Information Could Fuel Targeted Phishing Attacks

Although the attackers did not reach customers' encrypted vaults, the stolen personal information could still create opportunities for phishing campaigns.

With access to customer names, email addresses and account-related information, attackers could attempt to impersonate 1Password and send convincing messages designed to trick users into revealing sensitive credentials.

Scams don't come with typos anymore. The FBI's latest report counted 22,364 AI-related complaints and nearly $893M lost. 7 simple ways to protect your small business 👇 dlvr.it/TWSDCz #SmallBusiness #Cybersecurity #AIScams https://t.co/kMTpfXEHgw

— Fidextech® (@fidextech) November 24, 2026

Such attacks could take the form of fake security alerts, account recovery requests or messages warning customers about supposed problems with their accounts.

1Password has warned customers to remain alert to unexpected emails, text messages and phone calls that appear to come from the company.

The company has also emphasized that it will never ask customers to disclose their account passwords or Secret Keys. Users should only enter these details through the official 1Password application or website after navigating there independently, rather than following links in unsolicited messages.

As part of the Department of Justice’s Anti-Scam Surge, the Secret Service helped disrupt transnational scam networks by restraining more than $200 million in illicit funds, shutting down 1,780 scammer-operated domains and responded to 1,540 business email compromise incidents. Read more about the impact the Anti-Scam Surge is making at https://t.co/AeoCvpx0yi

— U.S. Secret Service (@SecretService) November 25, 2026

As an additional precaution, 1Password lengthened certain verification codes from six numeric digits to 10 alphanumeric characters, making them substantially harder to guess.

The company also contacted some users who had received emailed invitation or account recovery links, as those links contained tokens that warranted additional precautions.

1Password Strengthens Security Following Internal Breach

Following the discovery, 1Password disabled the affected employee GitHub account, removed the attacker's access and rotated internal credentials that may have been exposed.

🛑 North Korea-linked hackers have poisoned 7,600+ GitHub repositories to spread malware. The PolinRider campaign hijacks legitimate commits, uses Ethereum to conceal C2 infrastructure, and can trigger malware simply by opening a project in VS Code. How it works: https://t.co/0pbNFpXsY4

— The Hacker News (@TheHackersNews) November 26, 2026

The company said it had found no evidence of customer account takeovers or compromises resulting from the incident.

The breach also draws attention to 1Password's role in the cryptocurrency sector. In 2022, the company partnered with crypto wallet provider Phantom, allowing users to store wallet passwords and recovery phrases in their 1Password accounts.

However, neither the company disclosures nor the reports indicate that Phantom wallets or cryptocurrency recovery phrases were compromised in this incident.

For now, the breach appears to have exposed customer information and internal company assets rather than the encrypted vaults that hold users' most sensitive credentials.

— Crypto Banter (@crypto_banter) November 26, 2026

Nevertheless, the incident underscores how attackers can exploit a single compromised employee account to penetrate internal systems, steal customer information and potentially expose critical infrastructure.

While 1Password's encryption protections prevented the attackers from accessing customer vaults, the stolen information could still become a powerful tool for targeted phishing attempts, leaving users with another security threat to watch for.

The companies involved fall into two categories.

DayOne and Bridge are data center operators responsible for building data centers, providing power, and renting out server racks.

Bridge is backed by Bain Capital, and its connection to China stems from Chindata. Bain merged Bridge into Chindata in 2019, privatized Chindata in 2023, and subsequently sold its China business to a consortium led by Dongyangguang for approximately $4 billion, retaining only its overseas operations. Drew Chen, who became co-CEO of Bridge this November, is a founding member of Bain's Asian private equity team. Bridge's tenants are also changing. In February of this year, Bridge informed its lenders that the 68.4 megawatts originally allocated to Megaspeed had been transferred to Zenlayer. Zenlayer, headquartered in Los Angeles, is considered a US company under the new regulations, but its founder, Joe Zhu, was formerly a senior vice president at ChinaCache. The company has teams in Shanghai, Hangzhou, and Beijing, and its Series B funding was led by Guangyuan Capital. Guangyuan Capital, spun out of the state-owned enterprise China Everbright, also appeared in DayOne's Series C investors. DayOne is the overseas business spun off from GDS Holdings. According to the prospectus, GDS gradually retreated to a minority shareholder position, converting its loans to DayOne into shares, ceasing consolidation by the end of 2024, and terminating trademark licensing and customer referrals by the end of 2025. In January of this year, DayOne spent $385 million to repurchase a portion of GDS's shares, reducing GDS's stake to 19.4%. After GDS's withdrawal, three other companies held similar stakes. At the time of the prospectus submission, the top four shareholders were Coatue and Hillhouse Capital (19.5% each), GDS (19.4%), and Zhongfang Capital (15.6%). Hillhouse Capital has been a shareholder since its Series A round. When Wanguo Securities announced its Series A round in March 2024, the listed investors included Hillhouse Capital and its real asset platform Rava Partners, as well as Boyu Capital and other institutions. Hillhouse's shares are currently pledged to a group of lenders, and DayOne's CFO worked at Hillhouse from 2023 to 2026. Zhongfang Capital is one of the largest shareholders. According to the prospectus, its four holding entities subscribed for approximately US$1.16 billion in total, with the US$210 million investment in the Series A round being the largest single investment in that round. This shareholder's office is in Taipei, and its controlling shareholder is Chen Zhuwang. He is the eldest grandson of Wang Yung-ching and the nephew of Wang Xuehong. He joined VIA Technologies in 1996 and served as CEO of VIA China. The board of directors includes representatives from both VIA Technologies and Alibaba. VIA Technologies founder Huang Wei remains a director, holding approximately 3.5% of the stock options. Andy Okada is the president of the SoftBank-Alibaba joint venture and also the CEO of Alibaba Japan. The chairman and CEO are from the Temasek Group. Chairman Lim Ah Doo served on the board of ST Telemedia and its subsidiary STT GDC for over a decade, while CEO Jamie Khoo was a senior finance executive at ST Telemedia before joining VIA Technologies. ST Telemedia is a Temasek subsidiary and still held approximately 29% of VIA Technologies' Class A shares as of the end of March this year. Alejandro Aguzín, a new director this year, served as CEO of the Hong Kong Stock Exchange from 2021 to 2024, and prior to that, as CEO of JPMorgan Chase Asia Pacific. Revenue primarily comes from one client. The prospectus states that in 2025, 69.4% of revenue will come from "a technology company with a leading short video platform," whose contracted capacity has increased from 64 MW to 838 MW. The prospectus also states that two of the company's existing clients are on the Pentagon's list of "Chinese military enterprises." Tencent was added to this list in January 2025, and Alibaba in June of this year. Another type of company that comes forward is Neocloud, which buys its own chips, builds its own clusters, and then rents out its computing power to large companies on an hourly basis. The borrower of the frozen loan mentioned at the beginning, Aolani, is one such company. Aolani has been renting H100 servers to ByteDance in Malaysia since February 2025, and this year it prepared approximately 36,000 B200 servers for ByteDance. Its holding company is registered in the Cayman Islands, and its early investor is Singapore's K3 Ventures. K3's founder, Guo Mengxiong, is the grandson of Robert Kuok, and according to his resume disclosed in companies such as TVS Motor, he is also a director of ByteDance's Singapore entity. Aolani's servers are purchased from Aivres. Aivres was formerly Inspur Systems, Inspur's US subsidiary, and was renamed in 2023. Financial reports and US court documents show that Aivres is indirectly wholly owned by Inspur Information through Hong Kong's KAYTUS Holdings and the British Virgin Islands' KAYTUS Group. According to The New York Times, from April 2024 to February of this year, Aivres shipped at least $5.6 billion worth of servers to Southeast Asia. Inspur Group was added to the Entity List in March 2023, and Inspur Information was added last March; Aivres itself is not on the list. The US "50% related-party rule" is currently suspended until January 10th of next year. Once the rule is reinstated, subsidiaries of companies listed with more than half their shares will be subject to control, including Aivres, which is 100% owned by Inspur Information. GMI Cloud is also known as NeoCloud. Founder Ye Weiyan is the son of Ye Jiawen, co-founder of Realtek Semiconductor. The company initially focused on Bitcoin computing power, and its Series A investors included the Thai energy group Banpu. The Thai data center it used to buy chips for Tencent was hosted by STT GDC's Thai joint venture. STT GDC originally belonged to ST Telemedia, but was acquired by KKR and Singtel from Temasek in September of this year. The Thai joint venture's 51% stake is held by Frasers Property, a subsidiary of the Su Xuming family's TCC Group. Bridge replaced Megaspeed, which is backed by Alibaba. Alibaba was Megaspeed's founding anchor customer. In June 2024, Alibaba's Singapore subsidiary Apex lent money to Megaspeed's Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix, with Speedmatrix pledging its entire business to Apex. According to The New York Times, most of Speedmatrix's chips also come from Aivres, running for Alibaba in YTL's Johor data center. YTL calls this claim "speculation and unfounded." YTL, mentioned above, was NVIDIA's earliest partner in Malaysia. In December 2023, Jensen Huang visited Kuala Lumpur and announced an AI infrastructure collaboration with YTL. YTL now claims that its GPU business has only one 10-megawatt NVIDIA DGX Cloud project, fully funded by NVIDIA; the rest are managed and it does not provide GPU services to Chinese customers. There is another data center in Johor that was not mentioned in this report. Bitdeer, founded by Bitmain founder Jihan Wu, has a data center called A201 there, where they purchased over 100 racks of GB300 computing power, scheduled to be powered on early next year. Bitdeer says that over 70% of the capacity has already been committed by customers, with five-year contracts exceeding $1.7 billion, and the money for the cards mainly comes from customer prepayments. According to the New York Times, the computing power of this data center was planned to be sold to a Chinese tech giant. After the new regulations were introduced, brokerage firm StoneX estimated that there was a 25% chance that A201 would not be sold. The companies that lent them the money to buy the cards were mostly borrowed. Banks lent money to operators to buy chips, with the chips used as collateral, and long-term leases from large manufacturers serving as the source of repayment. Aolani's $480 million loan was calculated based on a debt service coverage ratio of 1.15. According to Natixis, syndicated loans for ASEAN data centers have totaled approximately US$48 billion since 2023. From major companies to operators, Citigroup and JPMorgan Chase have been involved in almost every stage.

In 2025, DayOne held a RM15 billion syndicated loan signing ceremony with several banksImage source: UOB

In September of this year, they led a $29.6 billion loan to ByteDance, unsecured, SOFR plus 68 basis points.

This September, they led a $29.6 billion loan to ByteDance, unsecured, SOFR plus 68 basis points.

For Bridge's $2.8 billion loan last year, each of them contributed approximately $120 million. This data center serves both ByteDance and has a service contract with Megaspeed. Bain Capital also handled the sale of at least 40% of Bridge's equity in April of this year. Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan Chase were the lead underwriters for DayOne's IPO, with Citigroup also involved; JPMorgan Chase is also the depositary bank for its American Depositary Shares. Singaporean banks were responsible for lead management and distribution. DBS was the lead underwriter for Aolani's loan, and three Singaporean banks were involved in DayOne's approximately $3.7 billion loan in Johor this October. Chinese banks have always been present; the closer they are to ByteDance, the more money they contribute. Of ByteDance's $29.6 billion loan, 15 Chinese banks contributed $18.9 billion, accounting for 64%. Further down the chain, at the telecom operator level, there are also Chinese banks. The $2.8 billion loan to Bridge includes Bank of China and China Minsheng Bank, and Industrial Bank also stated in a press release that it was the lead bank for one of Bridge's overseas syndicated loans. For Epoch Digital's data center in Johor, a $488 million loan was led by Bank of China and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB). The AIIB's project page states that the first phase of 60 megawatts was entirely contracted to ByteDance's BytePlus. For a data center in Rayong, Thailand, where ByteDance is the main tenant, the first phase loan was led by China Merchants Bank. Nvidia is also helping these companies borrow money, in a way that involves providing guarantees. For GMI Cloud's GPU loan in Taiwan, Nvidia promised to lease idle computing power at an agreed price for six years, while taking half of the revenue GMI earns from other customers. For Zankore's $3.1 billion loan in Indonesia, Nvidia provided revenue sharing and credit support. These guarantees, as far as we can see, have all been given to projects whose clients are not Chinese companies. Nvidia's equity investments are not so clearly defined. It is a shareholder of GMI and also of the UK-based neocloud Nscale, participating in several rounds of Nscale's financing since September 2025. In Nscale's IPO filing this year, it also committed to subscribing to $2 billion in convertible bonds. Of Nscale's $33 million in revenue in 2025, approximately 73% came from ByteDance's Singapore subsidiary, Spring. This proportion dropped to 52% in the first half of this year, and Nscale expects it to fall below 20% for the full year. The new regulations, effective November 16th, are based on the customer's headquarters. Regardless of the country where a data center is located, if it provides more than 12 million TPPs of computing power (approximately 750 H100 servers) to a company headquartered in or ultimately with a parent company in China, or if Chinese customers account for more than half of the total computing power, a license is required to supply chips. Existing data centers must obtain licenses within 90 days, with a deadline of February 17, 2027. This rule could have been much more lenient. Reportedly, Commerce Secretary Lutnick's original version only addressed future shipments, requiring only reporting for Chinese customers training models, and had a higher threshold. That version would have allowed Bitdeer's A201, and Lutnick's Cantor Fitzgerald was the sales agent for Bitdeer's potential $1 billion share issuance. Between Cantor and Bitdeer lies stablecoin giant Tether. Cantor acquired approximately 5% of Tether's shares in 2024. In May of the same year, Tether invested $100 million in Bitdeer, with Cantor also acting as the placement agent for that transaction. By June of this year, Tether held approximately 19.7% of Bitdeer's Class A shares. After Lutnick transferred his Cantor shares to a trust for his children, Tether provided a loan to that trust, with collateral including more than half of Cantor's equity. The final version released was stricter. According to Politico, it was pushed by Treasury Secretary Bessant, with Rubio on his side. Bessant stated that the Treasury Department had been advocating for Megaspeed to be added to the Entity List for months, but "the pen is in the hands of the Commerce Department." A week after the new rules were released, on November 23, seven companies, including Megaspeed, Speedmatrix, and Alibaba's Apex, were added to the Entity List. There are three details in the rules specifically targeting the practice of having someone else purchase the cards on their behalf. The first point concerns "indirect buyers." The rule states that the 2023 regulation, as determined by headquarters, "never applies only" to the direct recipient. Chinese companies, whether direct or indirect buyers in a transaction, or the sole or primary user of a data center, are also subject to this regulation. Large companies that prepay rent or lend money to operators may be considered indirect buyers. The second point concerns retroactive application. Law firm Paul Weiss interprets this as BIS believing that this regulation has been in effect since November 2023, and transactions from the past three years may constitute violations, thus encouraging companies to proactively disclose such information. The third point concerns exemptions for referral systems. Computing power used solely for recommendation systems does not require a license, provided that the data center reports the names of Chinese clients, their computing power usage, and the due diligence conducted to the BIS. This information is then forwarded to the End-User Review Committee, which determines the Entity List. The rules gave 90 days, and the banks began taking action within a week. The banks acted so quickly because financing itself may be illegal. Section 10 of the U.S. Export Administration Regulations (Export Administration Regulations) lists "financing" as a prohibited activity; regardless of whether one is a U.S. citizen or not, knowingly providing financing in violation of regulations can lead to prosecution. In October 2024, the BIS issued compliance guidelines specifically to financial institutions, with civil penalties up to twice the transaction amount. Applied Materials was fined $252.5 million in February of this year under this standard. We found no precedent for BIS to punish banks based on this injunction. However, once the rule is applied retroactively, banks will need to re-examine not only new loans but also funds already disbursed. Bloomberg also mentioned that some older loans may be deemed to have violated loan terms.

DBS signage outside the DBS building in Singapore

Image source: DBS

On November 18th, Citigroup and JPMorgan Chase added a clause to their Bridge loans stating that violations of US export controls would constitute default. This decision came from the two banks' New York headquarters.

Regional banks like DBS earn lead generation and distribution fees, provided they can sell the loans and transfer the risk.

The market for taking over loans was already tight this year. HSBC and Deutsche Bank were both transferring risk for data center loans, and Barclays was seeking insurance for over $10 billion in AI infrastructure credit, with insurance companies' underwriting capacity "nearly exhausted." After the new regulations, a risk transfer of approximately $1 billion by UOB also slowed down. A Singaporean syndicated banker interviewed by IFR said that no one was willing to commit even $100 million until the rules were clear. Interest rates also varied significantly. ByteDance borrowed its own money at SOFR plus 68 basis points; AirTrunk's general data center loan in Malaysia was at SOFR plus 225 basis points; Zankore's GPU loan customer was a US fintech company, backed by Nvidia, at SOFR plus 330 basis points. The same GMI, with Nvidia backing its loan in Taiwan, had an interest rate of approximately 3.43%. The expected yield on Tencent's chip purchase in Thailand is in the teens, but the draft term sheet states that Tencent must repay the loan in full early if it is added to the US restricted list. Smaller neoclouds in the US without credit ratings borrow at approximately SOFR plus 800 to 900 basis points. Tencent itself has a Moody's A1 and S&P A+ rating, yet the pricing for GPU loans using Tencent as a tenant is similar to that of small, unrated US companies. The three companies' situations differ: they acquire computing power overseas in different ways, and the impact they face is also different. ByteDance has the largest footprint. According to SemiAnalysis estimates, ByteDance alone uses about one-fifth of the computing power delivered in China. According to the Straits Times, citing industry and government sources, ByteDance leases about 90% of the computing capacity in Johor, mostly CPUs, running services like TikTok, which largely qualify for exemptions for recommendation systems. The AI ​​portion cannot qualify; the 60 megawatts signed with BytePlus are for enterprise AI cloud, and Aolani's 36,000 B200 chips are for training. This portion of computing power is constrained, and ByteDance lacks its own chips to fill the gap. It is the only major Chinese platform without commercially available AI acceleration chips. According to LatePost, ByteDance's AI chip was taped out this year, but its performance did not meet standards, and Shi Yunfeng, who was in charge of the AI ​​chip, has resigned. ByteDance's confidence comes from its financial resources; nearly two-thirds of its $29.6 billion loan came from Chinese banks, making it the most capable of bearing the risk itself among the three. Besides acting as a tenant, Alibaba also directly lent money to telecom operators through Apex, using the operators' entire business as collateral. According to the new regulations' definition of "indirect buyer," this is precisely the practice most easily traced. Apex also became the first subsidiary of the three major companies to be added to the Entity List. However, Alibaba has not scaled back its overseas operations. The day after the new regulations were released, Alibaba Cloud announced in Hong Kong that it would build new data centers in nine locations within a year, including Malaysia and Brazil, both of which are among the five countries specifically mentioned in the new regulations where shipments require licenses. Alibaba is still betting on Pingtouge (a chip manufacturer). Wu Yongming stated in a conference call that Pingtouge chips can support ultra-large-scale training, and the new generation Zhenwu V900 will enter mass production in the first quarter of next year. Morgan Stanley estimates that Alibaba wants to increase the proportion of its self-developed chips in its computing power from over 10% to 40-50%. [Image caption: Inside Tencent's Gui'an Qixing Data Center in Guizhou] [Image source: Cailian Press] [Image caption: Tencent's pressure lies in cash.] It operates on a prepayment model. In the third quarter, Tencent's free cash flow was negative 69.1 billion yuan. The company stated that excluding prepayments for computing power, it was positive 16.9 billion yuan, meaning approximately 86 billion yuan was prepaid in one quarter. At the end of June, Tencent had net cash of 58.2 billion yuan, which turned into net debt of 13.7 billion yuan by the end of September. The largest prepayment went to Oracle. For five years, approximately 100,000 Nvidia chips were placed in Oracle's Southeast Asian data centers, a contract worth approximately $7 billion, with Tencent prepaying about 30%. According to the Financial Times, after US officials "expressed concerns," Oracle canceled the agreement in early November. One of Oracle's data centers in Southeast Asia was leased from DayOne. According to Bloomberg, Oracle became the sole tenant of DayOne's Nongsa campus in Batam, Indonesia, in 2025. Oracle also holds a 15% stake in TikTok's US joint venture and is its security partner. Tencent also has a presence in Japan and Australia that has run into problems. Datasection, listed in Tokyo, derives 90.7% of its revenue in fiscal year 2026 from a company called NowNaw Japan. According to a Financial Times report last December, NowNaw's end customer is Tencent, involving contracts exceeding $1.2 billion in Tokyo and Sydney. Tencent responded at the time that its use of cloud services complies with applicable laws. In August of this year, an additional order worth 79.86 billion yen was cancelled. On November 16th, Datasection further slashed its revenue forecast for the current fiscal year from 162.2 billion yen to 17.3 billion yen. The landlord of the Sydney data center terminated the lease after months of dragging out negotiations to switch from B200 to B300. Tracing back the companies that bought the cards, most of the names that can be found are familiar faces. Taiwanese and Southeast Asian Chinese family capital, along with Singaporean state capital, have been acting as intermediaries between China and the West for decades, involved in manufacturing, real estate, and ports, with money and goods passing through their hands. AI computing power is the newest category in this business. Chinese manufacturers have demand, and the West has chips and dollar loans. They offer a company identity acceptable to both sides, and a piece of land where electricity can be connected. This business requires choosing sides periodically. In November 1989, Wang Yung-ching visited mainland China for the first time and subsequently proposed building an integrated upstream, midstream, and downstream petrochemical zone in Haicang, Xiamen, known as "Project 901." The news caused considerable controversy in Taiwan, with Taipei intervening to retain the project, offering tax breaks and a $1.5 billion water supply facility, while also lowering land and water prices. In August 1991, Wang Yung-ching accepted the Yunlin Mailiao proposal, which later became the Sixth Naphtha Cracking Plant. In November 1992, he held a press conference announcing the suspension of the Haicang project. More than thirty years later, his eldest grandson's Zhongfang Capital became DayOne's fourth-largest shareholder.

The signing ceremony of the investment cooperation agreement between Microsoft and G42 in 2024

Image source: G42, published by The National

The most recent choice of sides took place in the Middle East.

In 2023, US intelligence raised concerns about the relationship between Abu Dhabi AI company G42 and China. In December, G42 CEO Peng Xiao told the Financial Times, "We can't do both." G42 subsequently stopped using Huawei equipment and sold its investments in China, including its stake in ByteDance. In April 2024, Microsoft invested $1.5 billion in G42; withdrawing from China was a condition G42 had privately agreed upon with the US government before this investment. The middleman's business has always been about exploiting loopholes in the rules. The loophole of remote access has been visible to all parties for three years. BIS expressed concerns in its rule explanation in 2023, Nvidia conducted compliance reviews of each cloud partner, and bank loan documents listed the tenants. Nvidia also stated in March of this year that the export rules "by design" allowed cloud deployment outside regulated countries. The new rules on November 16th closed this loophole. A new round of siding with different sides has begun. Aolani's CEO said that about half of the contracted amount now comes from Western clients. According to the Straits Times, four of DayOne's top five clients are not Asian companies. The B300, originally leased to Chinese clients, is being relisted for sale to American and Western European buyers. Nvidia, on the other hand, turned around even earlier, telling its partners two weeks before the new regulations were released that Chinese clients would account for up to 49%. In the first three quarters of this year, data centers and cloud computing accounted for 35% of the approved investments in Malaysia. It has already chosen sides once. In May 2025, a deputy minister announced the use of Huawei's Ascend chips to build national-level AI infrastructure. Just a week earlier, the US Department of Commerce stated that using Ascend anywhere in the world could violate US export controls. The next day, the Deputy Minister's office retracted the statement, with Anwar saying the announcement was "premature." Two months later, Malaysia began requiring licenses for the export and transshipment of US AI chips. Regarding the new regulations, Malaysian Minister of International Trade and Industry Johari said, "If you want to stay at the table, you have to follow the US rules." Singapore's Prime Minister Lawrence Wong stated, "We don't enforce US export controls, but we don't want Singapore to be used or abused as a conduit." Middlemen can choose sides, but ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent cannot. There are 82 days left until the license expiry date of February 17, 2027.

data.title: What exactly are we expecting when we anticipate a bull market?
data.description:
Author: Blockchain Knight, Source: X, @BlocKnight21

There's an interesting change in the crypto market. In the past few years, people were always shouting that a bull market was coming, but now,

more and more people are starting to wonder when the bull market will actually arrive?

This feeling is even more pronounced in the altcoin market. Bitcoin continues to break price records, but many altcoins have yet to recover.

So

What exactly are we expecting in a bull market?

Is it a general market rise, with all our assets increasing in value?

Is it the expectation of a repeat of the bull market, where simply buying any project can yield several times the return? Or is it the anticipation of a market brimming with opportunities, allowing you to seize a chance to change your wealth? Upon closer examination, these expectations may ultimately point to the same thing: what we miss isn't the bull market itself, but the joy of making money within it. However, the problem is that a bull market doesn't guarantee profits for everyone; it can even be the beginning of losses for many. When a market rally begins, early entrants reap the rewards, and the profit-making effect attracts more capital. As prices rise, market sentiment becomes increasingly optimistic, and previously ignored projects begin to gain popularity. Later, many people stop caring about the projects themselves and only worry about missing the next surge (FOMO). At this point, early entrants begin to cash in their profits, while latecomers continue to chase higher prices; the more bustling the bull market, the easier it is to overlook the risks. A 2023 study by BIS found that before and after the Luna crash and FTX bankruptcy, large investors tended to sell, while small investors were more likely to buy. This illustrates that a market upturn does not guarantee profits for everyone; a bull market offers opportunities, not a guarantee of returns. In a bear market, accounts shrink, holdings decline, and once-favored projects go unnoticed. Over time, people easily doubt their judgments and even question the future of the industry. A bull market, on the other hand, brings the opposite: accounts start to profit, social media buzz returns, past judgments seem validated, and people regain a sense of control. However, this happiness is often short-lived, as desires rise with increasing profits. Therefore, bull markets offer more of a peak experience than lasting happiness. After the bull market ends, people will start waiting for the next bull market, hoping for a similar period of joy. Instead of pinning their hopes on bull markets, it's better to focus on bear markets. What's truly worthwhile in a bear market isn't guessing where the bottom is every day, but rather **re-understanding the market:** Which sectors still have growth potential? Which projects still have real business? Which assets are worth long-term attention? True investing is a bit like farming: sow in spring, harvest in autumn. No one can guarantee that every seed will bear fruit, but if you don't sow, you won't reap in autumn. Patience is the key to a bear market, while determination is the shield in a bull market. Patience allows you to maintain focus and judgment even when there's no profit-making opportunity, while determination allows you to execute your plan even when everyone else becomes greedy. We can look forward to a bull market, but we shouldn't make it our everything. After all, bull markets always end, and only the profits we actually realize truly belong to us.
